rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-4 report the authors' own model runs (hybrid ConvLSTM + ECMWF S2S) trained on 2015-2018 and tested 2019-2022 over the Yangtze River Basin and central Europe, evaluated against ERA5 reanalysis, SMAP L4 and ISMN in situ stations (Figs 4-15).
rows.notes: The study only shows that a hybrid deep learning-S2S model improves 1-46-day SSM and RZSM forecast skill (PCC, ubRMSE, RMSE) relative to SVR, RF, ConvLSTM and S2S baselines. It reports nothing on crop yield forecasting, irrigation scheduling or any crop-production outcome; agricultural benefit is only asserted in the introduction and conclusion. Moreover, the soil moisture inputs are ERA5 reanalysis and S2S model output rather than satellite SSM retrievals, and no SSM-to-RZSM transformation is performed (the two layers are forecast separately). Soil moisture forecasting is at most a precondition of the claimed crop yield forecasting benefit.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-4 report the authors' own forecasting experiments (hybrid ConvLSTM + ECMWF S2S) over the YRB and EU, validated against ERA5, SMAP L4 and ISMN in situ stations (Figs 4-15).
rows.notes: The study demonstrates improved sub-seasonal SSM/RZSM forecast skill only; it does not test or report any climate-resilient agricultural management, drought-risk management or decision outcome. Mentions of drought early warning and agricultural adaptation are motivational statements in the introduction/conclusion, not results. Data are reanalysis and S2S model output rather than satellite SSM retrievals, and no SSM-RZSM transformation is evaluated. Soil moisture forecasting is a precondition of, not evidence for, the claimed management benefit.

notes: Full text available (some pages duplicated from the peer-review layout but legible). Study is a methodological soil moisture forecasting paper using ERA5 reanalysis and ECMWF S2S data with deep learning; it provides no agricultural outcome evidence for either claim.
